title: Saying no, there is, there isn't
topic: לֹא; יֵשׁ / אֵין; questions with הַאִם and intonation
why: You learn to make negative sentences with לֹא placed before the verb, to say there is or there isn't (יֵשׁ / אֵין), and to ask questions. With these tools, the present-tense sentences from the two previous lessons turn into real conversations.

Saying no: לֹא

You know לֹא (no). It's also used to make sentences negative, and it's simpler than in English: no \"don't\" or \"doesn't,\" no \"is not,\" just לֹא placed before the verb or adjective.

אֲנִי לֹא עוֹבֵד הַיּוֹם.I'm not working today (a man speaking). [ani lo oved ha-yom]
הִיא לֹא גָּרָה פֹּה.She doesn't live here. [hi lo gara po]
הַדִּירָה לֹא גְּדוֹלָה.The apartment isn't big. [ha-dira lo gdola]

To answer no to a question, people often say לֹא twice: לֹא, אֲנִי לֹא גָּרָה פֹּה (no, I don't live here). That's completely normal.

The trap: English puts \"not\" after \"is\" or \"do\" (\"it is not big\"). In Hebrew, לֹא goes right before the word it negates: \"the apartment not big.\"

", "

There is, there isn't: יֵשׁ, אֵין

יֵשׁ (yesh) means \"there is / there are,\" אֵין (ein) \"there isn't / there aren't.\" They never change: no gender, no number. And since there's no word for \"a,\" \"there is a balcony\" is simply \"there is balcony.\"

יֵשׁ מִרְפֶּסֶת.There's a balcony. [yesh mirpeset]
אֵין חָלָב בַּמְּקָרֵר.There's no milk in the fridge. [ein khalav ba-mekarer]
יֵשׁ פֹּה מַעֲלִית?Is there an elevator here? [yesh po ma'alit?]

You never say לֹא יֵשׁ: the opposite of יֵשׁ is אֵין.

", "

Asking a question

In speech, you just raise your voice at the end, like \"You live here?\" in casual English: אַתָּה גָּר פֹּה? (do you live here?). In careful writing, you can start with הַאִם (a question marker, a bit like \"is it the case that\"): הַאִם יֵשׁ פֹּה מַעֲלִית? The subject is never inverted, and there's no \"do\" or \"does.\"

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
מָהmawhat?
מִיmiwho?
אֵיפֹהeifowhere?
מָתַיmataiwhen?
לָמָּהlamawhy?
אֵיךְeikhhow?
מָתַי אַתְּ קָמָה?When do you get up? (to a woman) [matai at kama?]
לָמָּה הוּא לֹא בָּא? — כִּי הוּא עוֹבֵד.Why isn't he coming? — Because he's working. [lama hu lo ba? — ki hu oved.]

The question word goes first, then you keep the normal sentence order: \"when you get up?\" To לָמָּה (why), you answer with כִּי (because).
